title: Reflecting in the Reflection: Integrating a Socratic Questioning Framework into Automated AI-Based Question Generation
extended_summary:
This preprint addresses the problem of generating high-quality reflection questions for learning environments, a task that is pedagogically important but time-consuming and inconsistent when done manually by teachers. The authors argue that existing automatic question generation systems mainly focus on factual recall and do not adequately support reflective, metacognitive prompts.

To address this gap, the paper proposes a "reflection-in-reflection" framework that uses two LLM-based agents: a Student–Teacher agent that drafts and revises reflection questions, and a Teacher–Educator agent that applies Socratic questioning to coach revisions. The system takes as input a teacher-specified topic, key concepts, optional instructional materials, and optionally student level. The agents iteratively refine a single question until the Teacher–Educator signals that it is satisfactory.

The empirical evaluation was conducted in an authentic lower-secondary ICT context in Czechia, using instructional materials for 8th–9th grade students about how the internet works. The backbone model was GPT-4o-mini, and a stronger GPT-4-class model served as an external evaluator in pairwise comparisons. The study varied whether student level and supporting materials were provided and compared dynamic stopping with fixed-length refinement, then also compared the two-agent protocol against a one-shot baseline.

The main conclusion is that dynamic, context-aware refinement generally produces better questions than fixed-length iteration, and that the two-agent Socratic protocol outperforms the one-shot baseline, especially for relevance and depth. The gains are strongest when contextual information is supplied, though the authors note that longer fixed dialogues can drift off topic and that the structured protocol trades a small amount of surface clarity for better pedagogical alignment and deeper reflection.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint with an experimental comparison design and substantial quantitative evaluation, but it uses an LLM judge rather than human raters and does not report a randomized educational outcome study with learners. The evidence is informative but best treated as qualitative/engineering evidence rather than high-credibility causal evidence in K-12 classrooms.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful improvements in prompt quality, especially relevance and depth, but the study evaluates generated questions rather than downstream student learning or teacher productivity with measured effect sizes. The likely practical impact is promising but remains indirect and unquantified.

interventions.use_case: Two-agent LLM-based reflective question generation for teachers, using a Student–Teacher agent to draft and revise questions and a Teacher–Educator agent to provide Socratic coaching feedback in an iterative dialogue.

LLM-generated pedagogical feedback on candidate reflection questions, with the Teacher–Educator agent evaluating clarity, depth, relevance, engagement, and interconnections and returning targeted coaching questions rather than rewrites.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether AI-generated reflection questions are better aligned to an ICT topic (fundamentals of how the internet works) in an authentic lower-secondary setting. Compared with a one-shot baseline, the two-agent reflection-in-reflection protocol is judged substantially more relevant and deeper, with relevance preference indices ranging from 0.60 to 0.92 and depth commonly above 0.60 across context settings.
finding.measure: LLM pairwise judgments of relevance and depth for generated reflection questions

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to reduce teacher authoring time by automating the iterative refinement of reflection questions. The paper reports that dynamic stopping with contextual information consistently outperforms fixed 5- and 10-step refinement, suggesting a more efficient generation process than longer fixed dialogues, though no direct time metric is reported.
finding.measure: Protocol behavior and comparative quality of generated questions under dynamic vs fixed iteration regimes

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main pedagogical target is reflective, metacognitive question quality rather than student achievement. The two-agent Socratic protocol is judged to produce questions that are deeper and more reflective than a one-shot prompt, indicating stronger support for critical thinking and metacognitive engagement, but the study does not measure learner outcomes directly.
finding.measure: LLM pairwise judgments of depth and overall quality of reflection prompts
